intro: Back-to-school is the second-biggest shopping season in the US after the winter holidays. For 2026, the National Retail Federation's annual survey pegs the average **K-12 household** spend at **$863.86** — a record, with total spending expected to hit **$43.3 billion** — and the average **college household** at **$1,437.79**. The biggest line item isn't pencils: it's **electronics ($293.11)**, followed by **clothing ($250.29)**, **shoes ($174.01)**, and **school supplies ($146.45)**. This calculator turns those national averages into a personalized budget: pick how many kids you're shopping for, their grade level (elementary, middle, high school, or college), and whether a laptop or tablet is on the list, and get a category-by-category breakdown you can actually take to the store. Once you have the number, two moves stretch it further: time the purchases with your state's tax-free weekend using the [Sales Tax Holiday 2026 Calculator](/en/sales-tax-holiday-2026-savings-calculator), and fit the total into your monthly plan with the [50/30/20 Family Budget Calculator](/en/50-30-20-family-budget).
keyTakeaway: The average US family will spend $863.86 per K-12 household on back-to-school 2026 — and $293.11 of it is electronics. Skipping the device purchase (or timing it with a sales tax holiday) is the single biggest lever on the budget.

explanation:
## What does back-to-school actually cost in 2026?

The National Retail Federation's 2026 back-to-class survey (fielded with Prosper Insights & Analytics) puts the average **K-12 household** at **$863.86**, up from $858.07 in 2025, with total K-12 spending expected to reach a record **$43.3 billion**. **College households** average **$1,437.79**, up from $1,325.85 in 2025 — pushing total back-to-college spending past **$100 billion** for the first time.

### NRF 2026 category averages

| Category | K-12 (per household) | College (per household) |
|---|---|---|
| Electronics | $293.11 | $341.95 |
| Clothing & accessories | $250.29 | $182.39 |
| Shoes | $174.01 | — |
| School supplies | $146.45 | — |
| Dorm / apartment furnishings | — | $194.00 |
| Food | — | $153.91 |
| Personal care | — | $133.34 |
| **Total** | **$863.86** | **$1,437.79** |

## How this calculator scales the averages

NRF reports **per-household** averages (a typical surveyed household shops for roughly 1-2 kids), so the calculator applies two documented assumptions:

1. **Grade multiplier** (editorial assumption, not NRF data): elementary ×0.85, middle ×1.00, high school ×1.15. Younger kids need cheaper clothing sizes and rarely a personal laptop; high schoolers skew toward pricier electronics and brand-sensitive clothing.
2. **Sibling economies of scale**: the first child carries the full household base; each additional child adds ~65% rather than 100%, reflecting shared supplies, hand-me-downs, and one household printer/laptop serving several kids.
3. **College students** are budgeted at the full college-household average each, since dorm furnishings, food, and personal care don't share across students living separately.

```
K-12:   budget = category_avg × grade_mult × (1 + (kids − 1) × 0.65)
College: budget = college_avg × students
Electronics toggle: removes the electronics line entirely
```

## Worked example — two middle schoolers, with electronics

| Category | Base | ×1.00 grade | ×1.65 scale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clothing | $250.29 | $250.29 | $413.0 |
| Shoes | $174.01 | $174.01 | $287.1 |
| Supplies | $146.45 | $146.45 | $241.6 |
| Electronics | $293.11 | $293.11 | $483.6 |
| **Total** | | | **≈ $1,425** |

That's about $713 per child — close to NRF's household average, which makes sense: the survey's typical household has more than one student.

## Five ways to cut the number

- **Skip or delay electronics**: it's 34% of the K-12 budget. If last year's tablet still works, the budget drops by roughly a third instantly.
- **Shop the tax-free weekend**: 18 states waive 4-7% sales tax on clothing and supplies in July-August. Check your dates and caps with the [Sales Tax Holiday 2026 Calculator](/en/sales-tax-holiday-2026-savings-calculator) — in Florida and Tennessee even a $1,500 laptop qualifies.
- **Inventory first**: NRF consistently finds a majority of families start shopping before mid-July, but early shoppers also duplicate items they already own. Check backpacks, calculators, and uniforms before buying.
- **Spread purchases across paychecks**: clothing sizes don't change between August and October — buy fall clothes later and only the first-week essentials now. The [biweekly pay periods calculator](/en/biweekly-pay-periods-2026-calculator) helps map which August-September paychecks absorb the spend.
- **College: buy dorm items used or split with roommates** — furnishings average $194 and are the most resellable category.

## What this calculator does NOT model

- **Private school uniforms, fees, or activity costs** — those can dwarf retail spending and vary by school.
- **Regional price differences** — NRF averages are national; urban coastal families typically spend above average.
- **Tuition, housing, or meal plans** for college — this covers move-in retail spending only. For loan planning, see the [Student Loan Payoff Calculator](/en/student-loan-payoff-time-calculator).
- **Your actual cash flow** — the output is a spending benchmark; fit it into your month with the [50/30/20 Family Budget Calculator](/en/50-30-20-family-budget).

faq.q: How much does the average family spend on back-to-school in 2026?
faq.a: According to the NRF's 2026 survey, K-12 families plan to spend an average of $863.86 per household (up from $858.07 in 2025), and college families $1,437.79 (up from $1,325.85). Total US back-to-school spending is projected at a record $43.3 billion for K-12 and over $100 billion for college.

faq.q: What is the biggest back-to-school expense category?
faq.a: Electronics, by a wide margin: $293.11 per K-12 household and $341.95 per college household on average in 2026. Clothing and accessories come second ($250.29 K-12), then shoes ($174.01) and school supplies ($146.45). If you skip the device purchase, the K-12 budget drops by roughly a third.

faq.q: How much should I budget per child by grade level?
faq.a: Using the NRF 2026 household average as the base, this calculator applies grade multipliers: roughly $735 for an elementary schooler, $864 for a middle schooler, and $993 for a high schooler shopping alone (including electronics), with each additional sibling adding about 65% of the base thanks to shared supplies and hand-me-downs. College students run about $1,438 each.

faq.q: Is back-to-school spending higher in 2026 than 2025?
faq.a: Slightly, for K-12: $863.86 vs. $858.07 per household, driven by small increases in shoes, supplies, and electronics. College spending jumped more sharply, from $1,325.85 to a record $1,437.79 per household, pushing total back-to-college spending past $100 billion for the first time.

faq.q: Can I really save money with a sales tax holiday?
faq.a: Yes — 4% to 7% on qualifying items, depending on your state. On the NRF average $863.86 K-12 cart, that's roughly $35-$60 if most items qualify. Eighteen states hold a 2026 holiday; the big constraint is per-item price caps (commonly $100 for clothing). Check your state's exact dates and caps with our Sales Tax Holiday 2026 calculator.

faq.q: When should I start back-to-school shopping?
faq.a: NRF finds the majority of families begin by early-to-mid July to spread the cost across paychecks and catch early promotions. The sweet spot: buy first-week essentials and capped items during your state's tax-free window (late July-August), and delay fall clothing until September-October sales.

faq.q: How does the calculator handle multiple kids?
faq.a: The first child carries the full household-average base for their grade level; each additional K-12 child adds about 65% of that base rather than 100%. That reflects real economies of scale — shared glue sticks and printers, hand-me-down uniforms and backpacks. College students each carry the full $1,437.79 average because dorm and food costs don't share.

faq.q: What does the college budget include — is tuition in there?
faq.a: No. The $1,437.79 college figure covers back-to-class retail spending only: electronics ($341.95), dorm or apartment furnishings ($194.00), clothing ($182.39), food ($153.91), personal care ($133.34), and miscellaneous. Tuition, housing, and meal plans are separate — for financing those, look at federal student loans (2026-27 undergraduate rate: 6.52%).

faq.q: Are the grade-level multipliers official NRF data?
faq.a: No — NRF reports one K-12 household average without a grade split. The elementary ×0.85 / middle ×1.00 / high ×1.15 multipliers are this site's editorial assumption, based on the consistent survey finding that teens drive higher electronics and clothing spend. Treat per-grade figures as planning estimates, not survey data.

faq.q: How do I keep the back-to-school spike from wrecking my monthly budget?
faq.a: Treat it as a planned annual expense: divide your calculator total by 12 and set that aside monthly (about $72/month for the average K-12 household), or map it onto your August and September paychecks. The 50/30/20 framework puts back-to-school basics in 'needs' and brand upgrades in 'wants' — a useful line to hold when the cart grows.
